# Portfolio Risk and Return Analysis

A risk and return analysis of my own investment portfolio, built in Python and presented in Excel.

I've invested my own money since I was 14. I started with individual shares and now hold a Stocks & Shares ISA of six holdings at set target weights. In my Principles of Finance module (92%) I learned portfolio theory, CAPM and the Sharpe ratio, so I wanted to use them on my own money and answer two simple questions:

1. **Is my portfolio actually diversified?**
2. **Am I being paid enough return for the risk I'm taking?**

---

## Results at a glance

Three years of monthly data (December 2023 to September 2026), annualised.


| Holding                                 | Weight   | Annual return | Annual volatility | Sharpe ratio |
| --------------------------------------- | -------- | ------------- | ----------------- | ------------ |
| Global equity (Vanguard FTSE All-World) | 30%      | 18.1%         | 11.6%             | 1.24         |
| Emerging markets (Xtrackers MSCI EM)    | 20%      | 21.4%         | 15.9%             | 1.11         |
| Nasdaq-100 (Invesco EQQQ, GBP hedged)   | 15%      | 25.0%         | 18.2%             | 1.16         |
| Legal & General                         | 15%      | 9.9%          | 16.3%             | 0.38         |
| Semiconductors (iShares MSCI Global)    | 10%      | 45.3%         | 42.3%             | 0.98         |
| Gold (iShares Physical Gold)            | 10%      | 25.4%         | 19.3%             | 1.12         |
| **Whole portfolio**                     | **100%** | **22.0%**     | **13.6%**         | **1.34**     |


**The short version:**

- **Diversification cuts my risk by about a quarter.** The portfolio's volatility is 13.6%, against 18.0% if the holdings' risks simply averaged out, with no loss of return.
- **The portfolio beats every single holding on risk-adjusted return**, with a Sharpe ratio of 1.34.
- **My four equity funds behave like one big bet.** They have correlations of 0.72 to 0.85 with each other. Gold and Legal & General are the real diversifiers.
- **Returns came in bursts.** Semiconductors lost money in 2024, then averaged 9.0% a month in 2026.

## What I did



### 1. Got the data (Python)

- Downloaded month-end prices for all six holdings from Yahoo Finance using `yfinance`, adjusted for dividends and splits. Without that adjustment, Legal & General's return would be understated, because it pays a large dividend.
- Checked each ticker returned the right fund name before using it.
- Dropped October 2026, because the month wasn't finished when I ran the analysis.
- Checked for missing values and scanned every holding's best and worst month for bad data, such as a price switching between pence and pounds.



### 2. Calculated returns and risk

- Turned prices into **34 monthly returns** per holding.
- Annualised them:
  - **return** = average monthly return × 12;
  - **volatility** = monthly standard deviation × √12.



### 3. Built the portfolio

- Combined the holdings at my target weights (30/20/15/15/10/10) to get the portfolio's monthly returns, then annualised them the same way.
- Compared the portfolio's volatility with the weighted average of the holdings' volatilities, to measure how much diversification is actually doing.



### 4. Risk-adjusted returns

- Calculated the **Sharpe ratio** for each holding and the portfolio:
  > (annual return − risk-free rate) ÷ annual volatility
- Used the Bank of England base rate (3.75% at the time of the analysis) as the risk-free rate.



### 5. Correlation

- Built a correlation matrix to see which holdings move together and which ones actually spread the risk.



### 6. Excel report

- Exported the results from Python into Excel, with one sheet each for the summary, the correlations and the monthly returns. I reshaped the returns into long format so a pivot table could use them.
- In Excel, I built:
  - a **bar chart** of Sharpe ratios, with the portfolio highlighted;
  - an **XLOOKUP** tool that returns any holding's return, volatility and Sharpe ratio;
  - a **pivot table** of average monthly return by holding and by year.



### How I checked the numbers

- The portfolio weights add up to exactly 1.
- I hand-checked the first month's portfolio return (5.58% in December 2023) against the Python output.
- The pivot table's whole-period averages match the Python averages exactly, so Excel and Python agree.
- The portfolio's return equals the weighted average of the holdings' returns (22.0%), as it should.

---



## Findings



### Finding 1: Diversification cuts my risk by about a quarter

- If my holdings' risks simply averaged out, the portfolio's volatility would be **18.0%**.
- The actual figure is **13.6%**: 4.4 percentage points, or about **24%, lower**.
- The return doesn't drop at all. It stays at **22.0%**, exactly the weighted average of the holdings.
- Returns average out but risk doesn't, because my holdings don't all fall at the same time.



### Finding 2: My portfolio beats every holding on risk-adjusted return

- **Portfolio Sharpe ratio: 1.34.** The best single holding is Global equity at **1.24**, and the worst is Legal & General at **0.38**.
- **Semiconductors had by far the highest return (45.3% a year),** but a Sharpe ratio of only **0.98**, because its volatility was 42.3%.
- Looking at return on its own would have pointed me to the wrong holding.



### Finding 3: My four equity funds behave like one big bet

- **Global equity, Emerging markets, Nasdaq-100 and Semiconductors** make up 75% of the portfolio, and the correlations between them range from **0.72 to 0.85**.
- **Nasdaq-100 and Global equity (0.85):** both are heavy in the same large US tech companies.
- **Semiconductors and Emerging markets (0.84):** emerging-market indices hold big Asian chipmakers, so part of my EM fund is really another semiconductor bet.
- **The real diversifiers:**
  - **Gold** is close to zero with most holdings (−0.08 to 0.17), apart from emerging markets (0.38).
  - **Legal & General** is also low against everything (−0.08 to 0.29).
- So the 25% I hold in those two does a large share of the diversifying.

![Correlation matrix](images/correlation.png)

### Finding 4: Returns were concentrated in particular years

Average monthly return by year, from the pivot table:


| Holding         | 2024  | 2025 | 2026 (Jan–Sep) |
| --------------- | ----- | ---- | -------------- |
| Semiconductors  | −0.4% | 3.4% | 9.0%           |
| Gold            | 2.1%  | 3.7% | 0.1%           |
| Legal & General | −0.6% | 1.2% | 1.3%           |
| Global equity   | 1.5%  | 1.2% | 1.6%           |


- Semiconductors' three-year average hides one huge year.
- Gold did most of its work in 2025 and has been nearly flat in 2026.
- Global equity was the steadiest, which fits it having the best Sharpe ratio of any single holding.

![Pivot table](images/pivot.png)

## Limitations

I've tried to be clear about what this analysis can and can't tell you.

- **It's a backtest, not my actual returns.** It shows how my current holdings, at my current target weights, would have performed over the last three years. I haven't held this exact mix for that long, so my real return in Trading 212 is different.
- **It covers a short and unusually strong period.** 34 months is a short history, and these were very good years for tech, semiconductors and gold. The figures describe the past, not what to expect next.
- **Annualising by × 12 ignores compounding.** It's the standard approach for Sharpe ratios and portfolio theory, but a compound annual growth rate would be slightly higher.
- **The risk-free rate is a simplification.** I used today's base rate for the whole period, even though rates moved over the three years.
- **Currency effects differ by holding.** The Nasdaq-100 fund is hedged to pounds and the others aren't, so currency moves affect them differently.
- **Volatility treats a big rise the same as a big fall.** That makes it an imperfect measure of risk.
- **Two pivot table columns cover partial years.** 2023 is only one month (December) and 2026 is nine months, so I've left 2023 out of the table above.

---



## What I'd add next

- **Maximum drawdown:** the biggest fall from a peak, which is a better measure of downside risk than volatility.
- **Rolling 12-month correlations:** to check whether my holdings start moving together during sell-offs, which is exactly when diversification matters most.
- **A benchmark comparison:** to see whether my six-holding mix beats simply holding a single global tracker.
- **Compound annual growth rates** alongside the simple averages.

## Project files

```
portfolio-analysis/
├── analysis.ipynb            # Full analysis in Python, step by step, with findings
├── portfolio_report.xlsx     # Excel report: summary, chart, XLOOKUP, pivot table
├── portfolio_analysis.xlsx   # Raw export from Python (Summary, Correlation, Returns)
├── images/                   # Screenshots used in this README
├── pyproject.toml            # Dependencies
└── uv.lock
```



## How to run it

1. Clone the repo and run `uv sync` to install the dependencies.
2. Open `analysis.ipynb` and select the `.venv` kernel.
3. Run all cells.

Prices update every day, so your figures will differ slightly from mine. Mine are as at 14 October 2026.
